The English catalogue is explicitly an abridgement. Teams differed in terrain, visibility, access, collection and editing; vegetation and dense occupation impeded work, desert single buildings had meagre finds, and smaller undiscovered sites remain possible. Installation inventories were placed differently by section. These conditions prevent treating the sector counts as a uniform detection experiment.

Diagnostic sherds supply site dates. Slash categories represent difficult distinction or transitional material; paired periods joined by and were distinguished but their percentages combined. Some Roman jars belong to late Hellenistic/early Roman, and some Byzantine forms continue into Early Islamic. Medieval glazed/painted ware was not subdivided; Ottoman collection may be incomplete. Absence of prehistoric specialists explains the weak prehistoric record.

Site areas normally describe built settlement rather than adjacent agriculture or installations, with possible differences between surveyors. Map names are preferred, vague field names omitted; two grid systems and the 1968 enumeration convention are explained. Individual descriptions sometimes explicitly include installations, so their qualification overrides the general rule.

Magen dates the survey beginning to 1982 and describes four years including processing, five teams and more than 500 square km. He reports intended uniform recording and publication, while the editor's preface records practical sector differences. Rapid development and the combination of map-sheet reporting with a regional synthesis shaped scope; complete southern Benjamin maps are explicitly absent.

The English half-title has a heavily crossed-out library stamp referring to an accompanying map held in the University of Michigan map collection. This page does not supply that map. Internal period maps were inspected, but any separate accompanying sheet remains unverified and must not be claimed read.
